text:
## Foreword

Globally, 357 million new cases of these four (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis and trichomoniasis) curable STI’s are acquired annually mostly by people aged 15-49 years. Sexually transmitted infections (STI’s) remain a priority in HIV response. Some viral STI’s, like human papillomavirus (HPV), HSV2 and HIV, are still incurable and can be deadly, while some bacterial STI’s like chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis and chancroid are curable if detected and treated.
A strong STI response will not only alleviate the burden of STI’s but will also have a beneficial impact on other health issues.. The STI response needs to be integrated with different health programmes and needs to be applied across sectors, including through school-based health education.
The Ministry of Health (MoH) as mandated by the Government of Eswatini prioritize STI’s, because of the correlation with other illnesses including HIV. STI’s play a major role in new HIV infections if not early diagnosed and managed properly. It is essential, therefore, that STI’s are properly managed at the first point of contact with health services.
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a significant threat to STI treatment, particularly for gonorrhea, classified by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as a high-priority pathogen, and Mycoplasma genitalium, which exhibits resistance to first-line antibiotics. Multi-drug resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae has notably reduced treatment options. In response, the MfH is transitioning towards a bacteriology-driven approach, prioritizing testing where feasible to inform empiric treatment.
This strategy aims to improve treatment accuracy, minimize inappropriate antibiotic use, and mitigate AMR progression. While syndromic management will remain essential in resource-limited settings, laboratory confirmation will be promoted in well-resourced areas to ensure pathogen-specific treatment, strengthening STI control and supporting sustainable treatment.
This guideline for management of sexually transmitted infections in the Kingdom of Eswatini is building upon the vision of zero new infections, zero STI-related complications and deaths, and zero discrimination and it aims at ending the STI epidemic as a major public health concern. To address the limitation of etiological and presumptive diagnosis, the syndromic management approach to STI’s will be emphasized in the implementation of this guideline in all health facilities.
In line with the 2030 global targets, the guideline aims at 90% reduction of T. pallidum incidence; 90% reduction in N. gonorrhoeae incidence; ≤ 50 cases of congenital syphilis per 100 000 live births; Sustain 90% national coverage and at least 80% in every region in the country.
DR. V OKELLO
DIRECTOR OF HEALTH SERVICES.
MINISTRY OF HEALTH (MoH)

heading_path: Front matter > Background
text:
## Background

STIs affect both men and women, and almost half of all STIs occur in people younger than 25 years old. Exposure to an STI can occur any time you have sexual contact with anyone that involves the genitals, the mouth (oral), or the rectum (anal). Exposure to STIs is more likely if you have more than one sex partner or do not use condoms. Some STIs can be transmitted through other routes, such as by sharing needles or needle pricks, during pregnancy, delivery and breastfeeding. Others may be asymptoms but still infectious.
STIs remain a priority in the HIV response. They constitute a major health and economic burden worldwide, and account for a substantial number of economic losses that are sustained in developing nations due to various morbidities. Globally, WHO estimates that more than one million curable STIs are acquired every day among people aged 15-49 years, amounting to 374 million new infections of chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis in 2020. An estimated 8 million adults aged 15-49 years acquired syphilis in 2022, and approximately 520 million people in this age group are living with herpes simplex virus type 2 [15]. Prevalence of these infections is highest in the WHO African Region.
In Eswatini, the number of clients presenting with STIs at health facilities more than doubled between 2021 and 2024, rising from 11,129 to 25,351, and remained at a similar level of 25,221 in 2025. Women accounted for 62% of 2025 presentations and men 38%. The highest caseloads were recorded in Manzini (8,542; 33%) and Hhohho (6,478; 25%), followed by Lubombo (5,362; 21%) and Shiselweni (5,253; 21%). The burden is concentrated in young adults: adolescent girls and young women aged 15-24 years accounted for 5,483 presentations, women aged 25-34 years for 5,368, and men aged 15-34 years for 6,508 [16]. Eswatini also carries one of the world's highest adult HIV burdens, with adult HIV prevalence of 24.8% and incidence of 0.62% [17], and 6,701 new HIV diagnoses among 213,516 people tested in 2024 [18]. This overlapping epidemiology makes the STI consultation one of the highest-yield entry points for HIV prevention, testing and treatment [19].
The factors that determine healthy sexual behaviour are complex and context-specific. In Eswatini, behaviours that pose high risks for STI and HIV transmission include; Low levels of knowledge about STIs and HIV; Inconsistent condom use; Multiple sexual partners; Gender disparities leading to unequal power in sexual decision-making and Inappropriate health seeking behaviour for STIs. The 2025 national programme review [16,20] further identified inadequate syphilis and hepatitis B screening and treatment in antenatal care, and voluntary medical male circumcision coverage of 48% against a 70% target, as persisting service-delivery gaps in STI and viral hepatitis prevention.
Effective management is one of the cornerstones of STI control as it prevents the development of complications and sequel. It decreases the spread of these diseases in the community and offers a unique opportunity for targeted education about HIV prevention and other STI’s. Appropriate treatment of STI at the first contact between patient and health care provider is therefore an important public health measure.
The use of standardized national protocols is strongly recommended to ensure adequate treatment at all levels of the health care delivery. All health facilities that provide STI services should implement the STI service package as outlined in this guideline. The growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) necessitates a shift in STI management strategies, particularly for gonorrhea and Mycoplasma genitalium, which have shown resistance to commonly used antibiotics, limiting treatment options. The emergence of multi-drug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a WHO-designated priority pathogen of public health concern, underscores the urgent need for bacteriology testing to identify resistance patterns and guide appropriate antibiotic therapy. Laboratory confirmation nonetheless remains limited: fewer than 200 detections of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis combined were recorded nationally through molecular (GeneXpert) testing in 2025, concentrated in the 15-29 year age bands, against more than 25,000 clinical STI presentations in the same period [16]. These counts reflect the current reach of molecular testing rather than the true burden of infection, and the gap between clinical presentations and confirmed diagnoses underlines the need to expand testing coverage and strengthen STI laboratory reporting. While syndromic management remains fundamental, Eswatini’s approach now emphasizes specimen collection and bacteriology testing where feasible, ensuring pathogen-specific treatment to optimize antibiotic use, reduce treatment failures, and curb AMR development. The purpose of this guideline is to standardize and recommend harmonized provision of comprehensive, quality and client centered STI prevention and treatment services. The goal is to promote service uptake resulting in improved client outcomes and elimination of STI infection including related complications.

heading_path: Front matter > Rationale for the STIs guidelines
text:
## Rationale for the STIs guidelines

There are several challenges to providing effective STI services to the people who need them. Many people with STIs do not seek treatment because they are asymptomatic or have mild symptoms and do not realize that anything is wrong. Others who have symptoms due to stigma associated with STI’s may prefer self-medication or seek treatment at pharmacies or from traditional healers. Even those who come to a clinic may not be properly adhere or complete treatment course. In the end, only a small proportion of people with an STI may be cured and avoid reinfection. This Guideline aims to help increase the proportion of STI patients that are treated and cured through assisting health care providers to:
- Raise awareness in the community about STIs and how they can be prevented - especially among populations who may be at high risk.
- Promote safer sexual practices, including delaying sexual onset, consistent condom use and having one or fewer partners.
- Promote early use of clinic services to cure STIs and prevent complications. Teach people how to recognize symptoms and when to seek care.
- Screening for asymptomatic infection for all sexually active clients.
- Manage symptomatic STIs effectively. Follow syndromic management guidelines for STI case management.
- Counsel patients on staying uninfected after treatment. Encourage them to comply with treatment, assist with partner notification and treatment, and reinforce prevention.
A combined strategy of effective community interventions and improved clinical services can have a large impact on STIs and their complications. Better clinical services increase the number of people who are cured. More effective prevention in the community, especially when it reaches those at highest risk, can reduce the overall STI problem. The combination of strategies benefits everyone.

heading_path: Front matter > Target audience
text:
## Target audience

These guidelines will be part of a consolidated set of guidelines for the prevention of STIs and management of people with STIs that are intended for programme managers for STI prevention and control at the national level and the health-care providers at the frontline in primary, secondary and tertiary health-care facilities. For the programme managers, the guidelines will assist in deciding how to organize the services for providing STI care and to determine the distribution of equipment and commodities that ensure access to high-quality STI care for people. The guidelines can also be used as an advocacy tool for the financial and human resources required to deliver adequate, acceptable and equitable STI care for everyone who needs STI services. Similarly, these guidelines can offer guidance to policy-makers other stakeholders and partners in providing services for STI prevention, treatment and care.

heading_path: 1.0 National STIs Case Management > 1.1 Rational of national management of STI and Viral Hepatitis (VH) cases
text:
## 1.1 Rational of national management of STI and Viral Hepatitis (VH) cases

Effective management is one of the cornerstones of STI control. It prevents the development of complications, sequela and decreases the spread of these diseases in the community. Offers a unique opportunity for targeted education about HIV prevention and other STI’s. Appropriate treatment of STI at the first contact between patient and health care provider is therefore an important public health measure.
The use of standardized national protocols is strongly recommended in order to ensure adequate treatment at all levels of the health care system delivery. Standardized treatment facilitates training and supervision of health providers and, this in turn delays the development of antimicrobial resistance in STIs.
Etiological diagnosis: Ideally, the diagnosis of an STI is made by knowing exactly what organism is present by performing laboratory tests. Unfortunately, this method of e diagnosis is often expensive and requires sophisticated equipment and skilled personnel to carry out. This places constraints on time, resources, costs and access to treatment for the patients. In addition, test results may not be available during the consultation, thus requiring patients to return in one or two days. This is not feasible in many settings. The risk of developing complications is high and the period of infectivity is prolonged by this delay in therapy.
To enhance etiological diagnosis, sample collection should be integrated into routine STI care, where feasible. Specimen collection methods vary depending on the suspected STI and the site of infection. The following approaches can be used:
- Urine samples: Used for Nucleic Acid Amplification Testing (NAATs) to detect Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in both males and females.
- Urethral or endocervical swabs: Collected for gram stain, culture, and NAATs, aiding in identifying gonorrhea, chlamydia, and Mycoplasma genitalium.
- Vaginal swabs: Self-collected or clinician-obtained samples can be used for bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, and candidiasis testing.
- Blood samples: Used for serological tests (e.g., RPR or TPHA for syphilis, HSV IgG/ IgM for herpes, and HIV screening).
- Lesion or ulcer swabs: Collected for herpes simplex virus (HSV) PCR testing, syphilis dark-field microscopy, or Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) culture.
- Rectal and pharyngeal swabs: Recommended for high-risk populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM), to diagnose extragenital gonorrhea and chlamydia infections.
By incorporating sample collection into clinical workflows, healthcare providers can increase diagnostic accuracy, improve antibiotic stewardship, and contribute to AMR surveillance efforts.
NB: Please refer to the relevant Specimen Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for detailed guidelines.
Clinical diagnosis: This involves using clinical experience to match identified symptoms and signs to a specific STI. However, even experienced specialists often misdiagnose STIs when they rely only on clinical experience. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 studies found that a clinical (syndromic) diagnosis of genital ulcer disease detected only about half of syphilis cases (pooled sensitivity 52.8%) and fewer than half of herpes cases (43.5%), while being somewhat better for chancroid (71.9%); the authors concluded that relying on clinical diagnosis alone results in significant numbers of missed cases and that affordable point-of-care diagnostics are urgently needed (Loh et al., 2022) .

heading_path: 1.0 National STIs Case Management > 1.2 Clinical Presentation for Symptomatic STIs > Genital Ulcer Syndrome
text:
## Genital Ulcer Syndrome

1. Chancroid: raised rough edges, beefy.
2. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV): itchy, burning and tingling sensation, painful blisters, ulcer.
3. Syphilis:
- Primary stage firm: painless lesions (chancre) and self-limiting, may last up to 3 weeks.
- Secondary stage: non itchy pigmented lesions can show up on the palms of your hands and soles of your feet, all over your body, or in just a few places. You may also have mucous membrane lesions.
- Latent/late stage: gumma, and may affect the central nervous system.

text:
## Genital Discharge syndrom

1. Gonorrhea:
- yellowish discharge
- foul odour
- pain and frequency on micturition
- dyspareunia
2. Chlamydia:
- clear or cloudy discharge
- dysuria
- early in the morning the opening of the penis is often red and stuck together with dried secretions
- urgency in micturition dyspareunia
3. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease:
- Lower abdominal pain
- foul discharge
- fever >38 degrees Celsius
- dyspareunia.
4. Trichomoniasis :
- greenish yellowish frothy discharge accompanied by a fishy foul smell.
- dysuria,
- dyspareunia,
- frequency on micturition
5. Candidaisis:
- Curd-like discharge
- itchiness
- erythematous mucous membrane on affected area.
6. Bacterial Vaginosis:
- erythematous mucous membrane
- Greyish white discharge with unpleasant fishy odour.

text:
## Other STIs

1. Human Papilloma virus (HPV) warts : raised or papillary skin colored growth with a cauliflower like appearance, soft to the touch usually painless but may itch.
2. Mycoplasma genitalium: Mycoplasma genitalium (Mgen) is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) that can infect your cervix, urethra and/or rectum. Because Mgen often doesn’t cause symptoms, many people who have it don’t know it and unknowingly infect other people. Mgen is treatable with antibiotics
3. Neonatal Conjunctivitis: thick, often sticky, muco-purulent discharge, hyparaemia
4. Syphilitic Warts: flat, extensive clustered lesions, mostly on moist areas.
5. Iguinal bubo: unilateral or bilateral swelling in the inguinal region, its fluctuant, painful.
6. Pediculosis pubis: whitish nits on the base of hairs accompanied by itchiness.
7. Genital Scabies: burrows, itchiness erythematous lesions
8. Hepatitis B: Many people have no symptoms during the initial infection. Some develop a rapid onset of sickness with vomiting, yellowish skin, feeling tired, dark urine and abdominal pain.
9. Hepatitis C: Every long term of Hepatitis c starts with an acute.Acute phase presents with jaundice fatigue nausea fever and mass aches.chronic hepatitis usually has no symptoms and appear only after the virus damages the liver enough to cause them this may include bleeding easily bruising fatigue itchy skin and dark coloured urine confusion and wait loss
- NB acute hepatitis c does not always become chronic. some patients clear the infection from their bodies. this is called spontanious viral clearence
NB: Screen all clients for STIs.

heading_path: 1.0 National STIs Case Management > 1.3 Syndromic Approach:
text:
## 1.3 Syndromic Approach:

A syndrome is a collection of signs and symptoms. The numerous and different STI pathogens produce a number of syndromes, hence a syndromic diagnosis is made when the patient’s signs and symptoms are matched to a particular STI syndrome. Syndromic approach offers treatment for more than one pathogen so that antimicrobial therapy is effective against all the pathogens that commonly cause the syndrome.
This approach to diagnosis and treatment reduces costs and increases access to treatment. This provides a more practical and cost-effective intervention for reaching the majority of patients with STI’s, especially in resource-limited settings. Syndromic STI management has some advantages which include the following:
Improved diagnosis
Advantages
- Can be administered by a wide range of primary health care workers (clinical officers, physician assistants, nurses, midwives)
- Allows treatment of a symptomatic patient in a single clinic visit
- Cheap, simple and cost-effective
- Permits treatment of mixed infections
- WHO still regards it as an essential component of STI control, and it remains the standard of care in resource-limited settings where lab diagnosis is unavailable or slow.
Challenges
- Overdiagnosis and overtreatment can increase drug costs
- Risk of multiple-drug side effects, drug interactions, altered vaginal flora, and antimicrobial resistance - WHO now treats overtreatment as increasingly undesirable given worsening resistance and limited treatment options.
- Not useful for detecting infections in asymptomatic individuals
- Vaginal discharge poorly predicts cervical gonococcal/chlamydial infection; WHO acknowledges its vaginal discharge flowcharts have limitations for cervical infections.
- Leaves a gap in establishing antimicrobial susceptibility for patients failing first-line therapy, especially gonococcal infections.
Key message: The Ministry of Health recommends that all patients presenting with STI’s are treated using the syndromic management approach, but when available, guided with quality-assured rapid tests, bacteriological and molecular assays for STI laboratory diagnosis

- Vaginal discharge poorly predicts cervical gonococcal/chlamydial infection; WHO acknowledges its vaginal discharge flowcharts have limitations for cervical infections.

- Leaves a gap in establishing antimicrobial susceptibility for patients failing first-line therapy, especially gonococcal infections.

heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components
text:
## 2.0 Essential Components

- History taking: Includes demographic information, a behavioural risk assessment, and medical history to identify potential exposures and risk factors.
- Physical examination: Focuses on the genital, anal, and oral areas, along with a skin assessment, to identify lesions, discharge, ulcers, or other STI-related signs.
- Establishing a syndromic and/or etiological diagnosis: Syndromic management remains a key approach in STI care, but etiological diagnosis is increasingly emphasised through laboratory testing. Where feasible, specimen collection (e.g. urethral, vaginal, cervical, or lesion swabs, urine samples, and blood tests) should be undertaken to confirm the causative pathogen, enable targeted treatment, and reduce unnecessary antibiotic use, thereby helping to limit antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
- Curative therapy: Effective antimicrobials should be administered at the first point of contact to reduce transmission and complications. Given the rise in drug-resistant STIs, treatment regimens should be reviewed and updated periodically in line with local AMR surveillance data to maintain efficacy.
- Health promotion package: Education on STI prevention, condom use, partner notification, and risk-reduction strategies should be integrated into patient consultations. Patients should also be informed about AMR and the importance of completing the prescribed treatment course.
- Clinical follow-up and referral where necessary: Post-treatment review helps confirm treatment effectiveness and detect possible treatment failures. Patients with persistent or recurrent symptoms should undergo laboratory testing, including antimicrobial susceptibility testing where available, to guide alternative treatment and limit onward transmission of drug-resistant STIs.
By combining syndromic management with bacteriological and molecular testing and structured post-treatment follow-up, Eswatini aims to strengthen STI control, slow the development of AMR, and improve long-term patient outcomes.

text:
## Gathering Patient Information

Information gathering strategies:
- Explain that all information will be kept confidential
- Develop a rapport so the patient can feel relaxed and comfortable
- Explore the patient’s concerns by practicing active listening
- Use a dynamic discussion between you and your patient as a means of taking the history, which should include an assessment of the patients risk level
- Take note of nonverbal cues.

heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.1 History Taking and Assessing STI and HIV Risk > Patient information to be gathered
text:
## Patient information to be gathered

Collect the following information during your patient centered discussion:
1. Name
2. Age, Sex
3. Physical address
4. Marital status
5. Presenting symptoms
6. History of presenting symptoms:
   - Discharge: duration, consistency, odour, color and amount
   - Burning, urgency and/or frequency of micturition and colour of urine
   - Swelling and/or pain in the groin
   - Lesion: location (vaginal, anal and oral), pain, ulcer, blister, bruises, indurations, rash, cracking
   - Lower abdominal pain in women: painful vaginal intercourse (dyspareunia)
   - Rectal discharge or pain
   - Difficulties with urination or defecation
   - Itching and/or discomfort in the perineum, peri-anal, and pubic areas
   - Itchy /Non-itchy skin rashes or warty lesions
7. Medical and gynecological history:
   - Ask ll females if they have ever been screened for cervical cancer
   - HIV status and proof of status/ testing history
   - Any chronic illness e.g. diabetes mellitus, If HIV+ and whether or not on ART
   - Medication history
   - Any known allergi
8. Social history:
   - Substance use: Alcohol, tobacco, and recreational drug use — including type, frequency, quantity, and route of administration. Specifically screen for sexualised drug use (chemsex) and injecting drug use, both of which are associated with elevated STI, HIV, and hepatitis C risk. Use standardised screening tools in a routine, nonjudgmental manner.
   - Transactional sex: Whether the patient has exchanged sex for money, housing, drugs, or other needs, as this is a recognised STI risk factor, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa.
   - Intimate partner violence and sexual violence: Screen for current or past trauma, sexual abuse, or violence, as STI consultations may be the patient's only opportunity to access support and referral.
   - Psychosocial context: Living arrangements, employment status, and social support, which may affect treatment adherence, partner notification, and follow-up attendance.
9. Taking sexual history:
A sexual history should be taken from all patients before examination and management of their sexual health concerns. The patient must be assured that the information they provide is held in strict confidence. The clinical environment should be welcoming, nonjudgmental, and trauma-informed, as some patients may have experienced abuse or violence. The service provider should conduct a behavioural risk assessment, including:
- Partners: Number and gender of current and recent sexual partners, whether partners are new or regular, and whether partners have other concurrent sexual partners or known STI/HIV status.
- Practices: Sexual exposure sites (oral, anal, vaginal), specific sexual practices, and whether the patient meets partners through apps or online platforms — as these inform anatomical site-specific specimen collection and testing.
- Protection from STIs: Condom use with regular and/or casual partners (frequency and consistency), awareness and use of PrEP, and vaccination status for HPV, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B.
- Past history of STIs: Previous STI diagnoses, treatments received, recurrent symptoms, and whether partners were also tested and treated.
- Pregnancy intention: Whether the patient or their partner intends pregnancy, current contraception use, and need for reproductive health counselling.
- Additional risk factors: Transactional sex (exchanging sex for money, housing, drugs, or other needs), sexualised drug use (chemsex), and intimate partner violence or sexual coercion - as these significantly elevate STI acquisition risk and may require referral to additional services
10.Past STI history:
- Have you ever been tested for STIs or HIV? When was your most recent test?
- Have you ever been diagnosed with an STI? If so, which infection(s) and when?
- Were you the index patient or were you identified as a contact through partner notification?
- If you were the index patient, was your partner(s) notified, tested, and treated?
- Did you complete the full course of treatment as prescribed?
- Did you return for a follow-up visit or test of cure after treatment?
- Have you had any symptoms that keep coming back, such as discharge, sores, or pain?
- Do you know the STI or HIV status of your current partner(s)?
A thorough sexual history will guide appropriate risk reduction and prevention counseling. There are several barriers to open and frank discussions of sexual health issues between patient and service provider.
See annex 1& 2: A table on guidance for clinical history taking of STI patients.

text:
### Steps to consider while taking a Sexual History (flowchart)

START BY → Within the last three (3) months, have you had sex with.... MALE / BOTH / FEMALE
→ Consider exploring further whatever the choice. In your sexual encounters you had.... have you ever had? Anal sex / Vaginal/penile / Oral sex
→ (each) Receptive / Both / Insertive:
   - Receptive → Consider: oral, vaginal and anal STI. Ask about: pain, sores, ulcers, discharges, growths.
   - Insertive → Consider: penile and oral STI. Ask about: pain, discharge, sores, ulcers and growths.
   - Both → both of the above.
→ Consider: the appropriate syndromic flow chart and treat accordingly.

heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.2 Physical examination
text:
## 2.2 Physical examination

Before examining a patient, obtain consent, explain each step in advance, and ensure privacy and comfort throughout the examination. Adhere to safety precautions like hand hygiene, glove use, and safe disposal of sharps. Conduct examinations in a well-lit room, exposing only the area needed while keeping the patient covered. Communicate findings using language the patient understands, and perform all procedures gently with minimum discomfort. Have consideration of the client's choice in the sex/gender of the attendant as per provisions in the Health Act of 2023.

heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.2.1 Physical examination of the female
text:
## 2.2.1 Physical examination of the female

Conduct a systematic general examination, inspecting the skin, palms, hair, lymph nodes (cervical, axillary, inguinal), and external genitalia for rashes, ulcers, warts, discharge, or swellings, documenting the size, location, and appearance of all lesions. For female patients, perform a speculum examination to inspect the vaginal walls and cervix for ulcers, warts, and discharge, and offer cervical cancer screening (Pap smear or VIA) if not performed within the recommended interval. Follow with a bimanual examination to assess for adnexal masses, tenderness, and cervical motion tenderness. Note that speculum and bimanual examinations may need to be deferred if the patient has extensive, painful genital ulcers.

heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.2.2 Physical examination of the male
text:
## 2.2.2 Physical examination of the male

Inspect the skin of the neck, chest, back, hands, palms, lower abdomen, inguinal areas, and thighs for rashes and sores, and palpate the cervical, axillary, supraclavicular, epitrochlear, and inguinal lymph nodes for enlargement or buboes. Inspect the pubic hair for lice or nits, and examine the penis, including the meatus with foreskin retraction, looking for ulcers, warts, discharge, or other abnormalities. If no discharge is visible, gently squeeze and massage the urethra forward to express any discharge. Palpate the scrotal contents and inguinal regions, and document the size, location, and appearance of all lesions found.

heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.3. Laboratory testing
text:
## 2.3. Laboratory testing

Laboratory testing is essential for confirming STI and VH diagnoses, detecting asymptomatic infections, and guiding treatment decisions. Tests include rapid diagnostic tests, molecular assays, bacteriological culture, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, performed based on availability at each tier of the health system. Specimen collection may involve blood, urine, or swab samples depending on the suspected infection and anatomical site.

- Educate the patient on treatment adherence, promote correct and consistent condom and lubricant use, and counsel on abstinence during treatment.
- Offer HIV counselling and testing, PrEP, voluntary medical male circumcision, and cervical cancer screening as per national guidelines.
- Issue partner notification slips, emphasise the importance of partner treatment, and follow up on partner treatment status at review visits.

heading_path: 3.0 Health Promotion Package > 3. 1 Health education and risk reduction counselling
text:
## 3. 1 Health education and risk reduction counselling

STI Education and Risk Reduction Counselling: An STI consultation is a unique opportunity to provide education and risk reduction counselling to patients most at risk. This should be an interactive process that builds on what the patient already knows. Providers should demonstrate respect, compassion, and a nonjudgmental attitude throughout.
Key counselling messages should cover:
- Diagnosis and treatment adherence: Explain the patient's diagnosis, its implications, and the prescribed treatment. Emphasise the importance of completing the full course of medication (the right drug, right dose, right route, right time) and explain how poor adherence contributes to antimicrobial resistance, making future infections harder to treat.
- Risk reduction and safer sex: Discuss methods for lowering STI and HIV acquisition risk, including abstinence, mutual faithfulness, and correct and consistent use of male or female condoms with lubricants . Explore any barriers the patient @perceives to practising safer sex and identify realistic behavioural changes they are willing to make .
- Partner notification and treatment: Stress the importance of ensuring all sexual partners are notified, tested, and fully treated to prevent reinfection and onward transmission.
- HIV and related services: Discuss the risk of HIV co-acquisition, offer HIV counselling and testing, and refer to additional prevention services (PrEP, voluntary medical male circumcision) as per national guidelines.
- Follow-up: Encourage prompt health-seeking behaviour for any recurrent symptoms, and reinforce that reinfection is possible if partners are not treated or risk behaviours continue.
- Before closing, confirm three commitments with the patient: to complete their treatment, to reduce risky sexual activities, and to ensure their sexual partners are fully treated.

heading_path: 3.0 Health Promotion Package > 3.2 Condom promotion and supply
text:
## 3.2 Condom promotion and supply

- The STI consultation is a key opportunity to promote, demonstrate, and distribute condoms, as patients are more likely to be receptive to understanding their role in preventing future STI/HIV exposure.
- Demonstrate correct condom use and support patients with partner negotiation skills to encourage consistent use.
- Provide condoms at the point of care, advise on where to access further supplies, and refer to the National Condom Distribution Guideline for additional guidance.

heading_path: 3.0 Health Promotion Package > 3.3 Notification and management of sexual partner(s)
text:
## 3.3 Notification and management of sexual partner(s)

Partner notification and treatment is one of the most important components of STI case management. It breaks the cycle of transmission, prevents complications, and identifies asymptomatic individuals who would not otherwise seek care. All partner notification must be conducted confidentially, voluntarily, and without coercion.
Partner treatment strategies:
- Offer immediate treatment to all sexual partners of the index patient, even if asymptomatic, using the same treatment regimen.
- Where a partner is unlikely to attend in person, consider providing the index patient with a prescription or medication for their partner (expedited partner therapy), particularly for populations with casual partners.
- Assess all partners for additional STIs beyond the presenting infection.
Approaches to partner notification:
- Patient referral (passive): The index patient takes responsibility for notifying and referring their partner(s) for treatment, either through direct conversation, accompanying them to a facility, or providing a contact/notification slip. Success depends on the quality of counselling the index patient receives and the provider's communication skills.
- Provider referral (active): A health care worker contacts the partner(s) directly. This may be necessary when patient referral is unlikely to succeed, but requires the index patient's informed consent to protect confidentiality.
- Providers should discuss both approaches with the patient and agree on the most appropriate method. In some cases, a combination of both may be used.

text:
## STI and Viral Hepatitis prevention interventions

STI and Viral Hepatitis Prevention:
- Promote abstinence, delayed sexual debut, and mutual faithfulness as key prevention strategies.
- Ensure availability and correct use of male and female condoms for all sexually active individuals, particularly high-risk groups.
- Encourage periodic STI screening for sexually active individuals, especially those not using protection consistently.
- Provide education on STI and viral hepatitis prevention and risk reduction.
- Reinforce universal precautions when handling hazardous waste and infectious materials.
Priority populations for hepatitis B vaccination:
- Health care workers and frontline personnel (police, firefighters)
- Pregnant women (from second trimester until delivery)
- Newborns (birth dose) and children under five
- Key populations, including people who inject drugs
- HBV seronegative individuals receiving dialysis or kidney transplant
- Unvaccinated sexual abuse survivors

heading_path: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH
text:
## 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH

Syndromic management remains the foundation of STI care in Eswatini, but WHO recommends that treatment be guided by quality-assured laboratory or point-of-care testing wherever such testing is available. Molecular tests - nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) - are the reference standard for Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Trichomonas vaginalis and Mycoplasma genitalium, and may be performed either in a laboratory or at the point of care using platforms already deployed in the Eswatini network, such as GeneXpert. Culture retains a specific and irreplaceable role for N. gonorrhoeae: it remains the only method that yields an isolate for antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and is therefore essential to national AMR surveillance. Where no aetiological test is accessible, syndromic treatment should still be given at the first point of contact and the specimen referred onward where feasible. The tests set out in this section are drawn from the WHO manual Laboratory and point-of-care diagnostic testing for sexually transmitted infections, including HIV (fourth edition, 2023), the 2024 WHO updated recommendations for the treatment of N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis and T. pallidum and new recommendations on syphilis testing, and the 2025 WHO guidelines for the management of asymptomatic STIs.

heading_path: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH > 4.1 Recommended diagnostic tests by infection
text:
### Table 2: Recommended laboratory and point-of-care tests for the STIs and viral hepatitis covered by these guidelines

| Infection / pathogen | Recommended test | Specimen | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhoea) | NAAT, laboratory or point of care (e.g. GeneXpert); culture where AMR surveillance is required | First-void urine (male); vaginal or endocervical swab; rectal or pharyngeal swab per exposure | Culture is the only method yielding an isolate for antimicrobial susceptibility testing. No quality-assured rapid test exists for NG alone. |
| Chlamydia trachomatis (chlamydia) | NAAT, laboratory or point of care | First-void urine (male); vaginal or endocervical swab (self-collected acceptable); rectal or pharyngeal swab | Reference standard. Serology is not recommended for genital infection. |
| C. trachomatis serovars L1-L3 (LGV) | NAAT with LGV genotyping at a reference laboratory | Ulcer swab, bubo aspirate or rectal swab | Refer specimen onward; genotyping is not available at facility level. |
| Trichomonas vaginalis | NAAT preferred; POC antigen test or saline wet-mount microscopy where NAAT is unavailable | Vaginal swab; first-void urine (male) | Wet mount has low sensitivity - a negative result does not exclude infection. |
| Mycoplasma genitalium | NAAT, with macrolide-resistance markers where available | First-void urine; vaginal swab | Test only in persistent or recurrent urethritis or cervicitis. Do not screen asymptomatic people. |
| Treponema pallidum (syphilis) | Treponemal test (RDT, TPHA, TPPA or FTA) plus non-treponemal test (RPR or VDRL) with titre; dual HIV/syphilis RDT in antenatal care | Whole blood by fingerprick for RDT; serum for laboratory tests | WHO also recommends syphilis self-testing as an additional option. An RPR titre is required to monitor treatment response. |
| Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 | NAAT (PCR) on lesion material | Swab from the base of an unroofed vesicle or ulcer | Type-specific serology only in selected cases. Viral culture is insensitive. |
| Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) | Multiplex genital ulcer NAAT where available; otherwise clinical diagnosis | Ulcer swab | Culture requires specialised media and is not routinely available. |
| Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis) | Microscopy for Donovan bodies on a tissue crush preparation or biopsy | Lesion tissue | Culture is not routine. |
| Human papillomavirus (HPV) | HPV DNA or mRNA testing as the primary cervical screening test; VIA where HPV testing is unavailable | Cervical or vaginal sample (self-collection acceptable) | Anogenital warts are diagnosed clinically - no laboratory test is required. |
| HIV | Serial or parallel rapid diagnostic testing per the national algorithm; NAAT for infants | Whole blood by fingerprick; plasma or serum | Offer to every patient presenting with an STI, and retest per national guidelines. |
| Hepatitis B virus (HBV) | HBsAg by RDT or laboratory immunoassay; HBV DNA viral load to assess treatment eligibility | Whole blood by fingerprick for RDT; serum or plasma | HBeAg and ALT support staging. Test all pregnant women at least once per pregnancy. |
| Hepatitis C virus (HCV) | Anti-HCV antibody by RDT or laboratory assay; HCV RNA or core antigen to confirm viraemia | Whole blood by fingerprick for RDT; serum or plasma | Antibody alone cannot distinguish current from past infection. |
| Bacterial vaginosis | Vaginal pH and microscopy using Nugent score or Amsel criteria | Vaginal swab | Not an STI in the strict sense. No NAAT required. |
| Vulvovaginal candidiasis | Saline or KOH wet-mount microscopy; culture for recurrent disease | Vaginal swab | Clinical diagnosis is usually sufficient. |
| Scabies, pediculosis pubis and molluscum contagiosum | Clinical diagnosis; dermoscopy or microscopy of the mite or louse if uncertain | Not applicable | No laboratory test is required. |

heading_path: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH > 4.2 Specimen collection and transport
text:
## 4.2 Specimen collection and transport

Correct specimen collection determines the validity of every result that follows. Use only the swab and transport medium supplied with the test platform in use, label each specimen at the patient's side, and record the anatomical site sampled on the request form so that the laboratory can interpret the result correctly. Self-collected vaginal swabs perform as well as clinician-collected swabs for NAAT and should be offered where privacy allows. For extragenital infection, sample the site of exposure: a genital specimen will not detect pharyngeal or rectal infection. Where testing is not performed on site, transport specimens within the time and temperature range specified by the manufacturer and refer them to the nearest testing laboratory without delay.

heading_path: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH > 4.3 Antimicrobial resistance surveillance
text:
## 4.3 Antimicrobial resistance surveillance

N. gonorrhoeae has developed resistance to nearly every antibiotic used to treat it, and molecular tests cannot yet provide reliable susceptibility results from non-culture specimens. Sentinel facilities should therefore continue to collect urethral and endocervical specimens for culture and susceptibility testing, and results should be reported to the national AMR surveillance system so that first-line regimens in these guidelines can be reviewed against local data. Patients whose symptoms persist or recur after correctly completed treatment should be re-tested, and an isolate sought for susceptibility testing where possible, rather than being treated empirically a second time.

heading_path: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH > 4.4 Testing asymptomatic people
text:
## 4.4 Testing asymptomatic people

Most STIs are asymptomatic, and syndromic management cannot reach them. WHO recommends targeted screening for gonorrhoea and chlamydia in high-prevalence settings where resources allow, prioritising pregnant women, sexually active adolescents and young people aged 10-24 years, sex workers, and men who have sex with r. Screening for sex workers and men who have sex with men should be offered at least annually, and six-monthly where feasible. Syphilis and HIV testing should be offered to every person attending for STI care, irrespective of symptoms, and to every pregnant woman at her first antenatal visit. Hepatitis B surface antigen testing should likewise be offered to all pregnant women to allow timely antiviral prophylaxis and birth-dose vaccination.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.1 Genital ulcer syndrome (GUS), including anorectal ulcer > Description
text:
## Description

Ulceration of the genitals is among the most common STI syndromes in men and women. The most common STI’s presenting with genital ulcer(s) are genital herpes (caused by herpes simplex virus, syphilis, and chancroid. Individual ulcers may be caused by more than one pathogen (mixed infections). Other STI’s causing genital ulcers include donovanosis and lymphogranuloma.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.1 Genital ulcer syndrome (GUS), including anorectal ulcer > Recommended treatment regimens
text:
## Recommended treatment regimens

If ulcer(s) alone or ulcer(s) along with herpetic vesicles are visible* Treat for syphilis, chancroid and herpes. Regimen should include:
- Benzathine Penicillin*, 2.4 million units I.M STAT, PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1g orally STAT; OR Ceftriaxone 1g I.M STAT; OR Ciprofloxacin, 500mg orally BID for 3 days; OR Erythromycin, 500 mg orally QID for 7 days (to treat chancroid) PLUS
- Acyclovir, 400mg orally TDS for 7 days (to treat genital herpes).
NB: Penicillin-allergic patients treat with: Erythromycin 500mg 6 hourly for 14 days

text:

- First episode: Acyclovir, 400mg orally TDS for 7 days;
- Recurrent episodes: Acyclovir, 800mg orally TDS for 3days
The chronic and recurrent nature of the illness should be explained to the patient, who should be advised to avoid sexual contact until the lesions are completely healed

text:
## Treatment Options for Urethral Discharge Syndrome

Recommended treatment regimens for gonococcal infections
First-line:
- Ceftriaxone, 1 g IM STAT. OR Cefixime, 400 mg orally STAT,
Second-line:
- Spectinomycin, 2 g IM STAT, OR Gentamicin, 240 mg IM STAT.
Recommended treatment regimens for chlamydial infections
First-line:
- Azithromycin 1 g orally as a STAT dose
Second-line:
- Doxycycline 100 mg orally BD for 7 days
- Erythromycin 500 mg orally QID for 7 days
- Ofloxacin 400 mg orally BD for 7 days.
NB: For ano-rectal infection: Doxycline is preferred over Azithromycin
Recommended treatment regimens for trichomonas infection
- Metronidazole 2g orally STAT

text:
### Figure 1 syndromic treatment chart for male urethral syndrome (chart 3)

Patient complains of urethral discharge or burning on urination
→ Take history and examine. Provide HIV testing and counselling (opt-out).
→ Discharge seen or dysuria confirmed by clinical history?
   - NO → Any other STIs syndrome or illness present?
      - NO → Reassure, counsel and educate; condom promoted and provided.
      - YES → Treat according to appropriate flow chart.
   - YES → Ceftriaxone, 1 g I.M stat PLUS Azithromycin, 1 g orally stat PLUS Metronidazole, 2 g orally stat. Health promotion package and follow up after 7 days.
      → Follow up at 7 days: discharge or dysuria present?
         - NO → Reinforce health promotion package.
         - YES → Re-infection? Or poor compliance?
            - YES → Repeat treatment; reinforce health promotion package.
            - NO → Reassure, condom promoted and provided. Refer for further management.

Health promotion package:
- Educate, ensure compliance, and counsel on treatment.
- Promote abstinence or condom use during treatment.
- Promote and demonstrate consistence condom use and provide condoms.
- Issue one notification slip for each sexual partner and emphasize the importance of partner treatment.
- Offer HIV counselling and testing, as per Integrated HIV Guidelines.
- Offer male circumcision to the uncircumcised.
- Offer pre exposure prophylaxis as per Guideline.
- Provide cervical cancer screening during follow-up visit.

text:
### Figure 2 Point of care management of male urethral syndrome

Person with symptom of urethral discharge from penis → Take medical and sexual history and assess risk for STIs → Physical and genital examination. Then:
- Resources and capacity for molecular assays: Perform test → Are results available on same day?
   - No* → (go to the limited-capacity pathway: urethral discharge present?)
   - Yes → Is test positive for NG/CT?
      - Yes → Treat based on test results → Offer HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services.
      - No → Offer HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services.
- Limited laboratory capacity: Urethral discharge present?
   - Yes → TREAT for NG and CT → Offer HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services.
   - No → Offer HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services.
→ See patient in 1 week to see if symptoms persist or recur or contact sooner for treatment based on results of molecular assay.

NG, N. gonorrhoeae; CT, C. trachomatis.
* If molecular assay was performed and results were not available on same day, revise the syndromic treatment initially provided according to the test results when available.
# If test is negative but urethral discharge is present, treat for non-gonococcal/non-chlamydial urethritis (such as M. genitalium, T. vaginalis or herpes simplex virus).

Person with symptom of anorectal discharge and reports receptive anal sex → Take medical and sexual history and assess risk for exposure to STIs → Perform genital and peri-anal inspection (and anoscopy if available or digital exam if acceptable) (→ Refer for other investigations if anorectal discharge not related to STIs). - Resources and capacity for molecular assays: Perform test → Is test positive for NG/CT/MG?

   - Yes → TREAT for NG and CT → Is there pain? (Yes → TREAT additionally for herpes simplex virus) → Offer HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services.
   - No → Offer HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services.
→ Review in 1 week if symptoms persist or recur.
NG, N. gonorrhoeae; CT, C. trachomatis; MG, M. genitalium.

text:
## Syndromic treatment of vaginal discharge syndrome (VDS)

- Ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1 g orally STAT PLUS
- Metronidazole 2g orally STAT. NB : In case VDS is due to vaginitis, conduct risk assessment, if negative the treatment regimen should cover organisms causing bacterial vaginosis and candidiasis infections:
- Metronidazole** 2 g orally, STAT dose PLUS
- Clotrimazole pessary 500mg intra-vaginally once nocte Patients taking Metronidazole should be cautioned to avoid taking alcohol while on these drugs and up to 24-48 hours after the last dose.

text:
## Treatment Options for vaginal discharge syndrome

When risk assessment is positive, OR where speculum examination is not possible. The treatment regimen should cover organisms causing gonococcal, chlamydial and trichomonas infections.
- Ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT OR Cefixime 400 mg orally STAT PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1 g orally STAT (OR Erythromycin 500mg QID x 7 days) PLUS
- Metronidazole 2g orally STAT.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.3. Vaginal Discharge Syndrome (VDS) > 5.3.1 Chart 4 (Figure 4)
text:
### Figure 4 syndromic treatment for vaginal discharge syndrome (chart 4)

Patient complains of vaginal discharge/burning micturition or vulval itchiness
→ Take history and do risk assessment. Perform bi-manual examination and examine including speculum.
→ Abnormal discharge or vulval itchiness confirmed?
   - NO → Any other STI syndrome or illness present?
      - NO → Reassure, counsel and educate. Condom promoted and [provided].
      - YES → Treat according to appropriate flow chart.
   - YES → Ceftriaxone, 1 g IM stat PLUS Azithromycin, 1g orally stat PLUS Metronidazole, 2g orally stat. If candida is evident give clotrimazole 500mg pessaries intra-vaginally stat and follow up after 7 days.
      → Follow up at 7 days: improved?
         - YES → Reinforce health promotion.
         - NO → Re-infection? Or poor compliance?
            - YES → Repeat treatment and reinforce health promotion package.
            - NO → Refer for further management.

Health promotion package:
- Educate, ensure compliance, and counsel on treatment.
- Promote abstinence or condom use during treatment.
- Promote correct and consistent condom use also provide condoms and lubricants.
- Issue one notification slip for each sexual partner and emphasize the importance of partner treatment.
- Offer HIV counselling and testing, as per Integrated HIV Guidelines.
- Offer voluntary medical male circumcision.
- Offer pre exposure prophylaxis as per guideline.
- Provide cervical cancer screening during follow-up visit.

text:
## Description

Etiology
N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis infections among post pubertal women infect the endocervix rather than the vagina and can thus cause a cervical discharge, which may manifest as vaginal discharge. However, these two pathogens are less commonly associated with vaginal discharge.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > Cervical Infections > Examination findings - signs:
text:
## Examination findings - signs:

Speculum examination may reveal a normal-looking cervix in the presence of endocervical infection. For those with abnormalities, the cervix may be
erythematous or severely eroded and associated with a muco-purulent cervical discharge. The cervix may be friable and bleed easily on contact.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.4 Lower abdominal pain (LAP) > Description
text:
## Description

Lower abdominal pain is one of the major signs of Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) which may be accompanied by cervical motion tenderness on bimanual examination, a complaint of back pain, lower tenderness with or without guarding on abdominal examination.
All sexually active women presenting with a history of lower abdominal pain should be carefully evaluated for the presence of salphingitis and/or endometritis - elements of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). In addition, routine bimanual and abdominal examination should be carried out on all women with presumptive STI since some women with PID will not complain of lower abdominal pain. Hospitalization of patients with acute PID should be seriously considered when:
- The diagnosis is uncertain
- Surgical emergencies such as appendicitis and ectopic pregnancy cannot be excluded
- A pelvic abscess is suspected
- The patient is pregnant Risk factors: women with IUD have a higher risk of PID, particularly if the IUD had been inserted recently.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.4 Lower abdominal pain (LAP) > Clinical features
text:
## Clinical features

Lower abdominal pain is a complex syndrome to identify. Several other important non-STI causes may produce similar symptoms and signs.
- In all suspected lower abdominal pain patients, bi-manual examination and speculum must be conducted.
- The physical examination should assess the general condition of the patient. In all cases, pregnancy-related conditions, as well as an acute abdominal tenderness, should be excluded.
- Elevated temperature, high pulse rate, bleeding and low blood pressure, for example, should alert to the possibility of severe pelvic infection.
NB: Such patients should be referred urgently.
- On palpation, if signs of peritonitis such as lower abdomen guarding and rebound tenderness or if abdominal masses are present, the patient must be referred accordingly for further management.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.4 Lower abdominal pain (LAP) > Treatment options for lower abdominal pain
text:
## Treatment options for lower abdominal pain

- Ceftriaxone, 1g I.M STAT, Gentamycin 240mg IM Stat and Spectinmycin 2 grams IM PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1g orally per week for 2 weeks, OR Doxycycline 100 mg orally BID for 14 days OR Erythromycin, 500 mg orally QID for 14 days PLUS
- Metronidazole, 400mg orally BID for 7 to 14 days
NB: Patients taking Metronidazole should be cautioned against taking alcohol while on these drugs and up to 24 - 48 hours after the last dose.
Caution: PID can be a serious condition. The patient must be referred: if she does not respond to treatment within 3 days and even earlier in case there is worsening of her condition. Because of the high risk for maternal morbidity, fetal wastage, and preterm delivery. Pregnant women who have suspected PID should be referred for hospitalization further management by an obstetrician.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.4 Lower abdominal pain (LAP) > 5.4.1 Chart 5 (Figure 5)
text:
### Figure 5 syndromic treatment for lower abdominal pain (chart 5)

Woman complains of LAP with or without vaginal discharge
→ Take history including (gynaecological) and physical examination (abdominal and vaginal).
→ Any of the following present? Missed/overdue period or recent delivery/abortion/miscarriage? Abdominal guarding and/or rebound tenderness? Or abnormal vaginal bleeding?
   - YES → Do pregnancy test; set up an IV line; do resuscitation measures if necessary; refer for emergency medical care.
   - NO → Pain on moving the cervix? Or lower abdominal tenderness with or without vaginal discharge?
      - NO → Any other STI syndrome or illness present? (NO → Provide health promotion package and refer accordingly; YES → Treat according to appropriate flowchart.)
      - YES → Ceftriaxone 1 g i.M. stat PLUS Azithromycin 1 g PO/week x 2 weeks PLUS Metronidazole 400 mg PO bid x 7-14 days and advise to come early within 3 days, or earlier if worsening.
         → Follow up at 3 days: improved? (YES → Finalize treatment; re-inforce health promotion package. NO → Refer for further management.)

Health promotion package:
- Educate, ensure compliance, and counsel on treatment.
- Promote abstinence or condom use during treatment.
- Promote correct and consistent condom use also provide condoms and lubricants.
- Issue one notification slip for each sexual partner and emphasize the importance of partner treatment.
- Offer HIV counselling and testing, as per Integrated HIV Guidelines.
- Offer voluntary medical male circumcision.
- Offer pre exposure prophylaxis as per guideline.
- Provide cervical cancer screening during follow-up visit.

      - YES → Ceftriaxone 1 g i.M. stat PLUS Azithromycin 1 g PO/week x 2 weeks PLUS Metronidazole 400 mg PO bid x 7-14 days and advise to come early within 3 days, or earlier if worsening.

Health promotion package:
- Educate, ensure compliance, and counsel on treatment.
- Promote abstinence or condom use during treatment.
- Promote correct and consistent condom use also provide condoms and lubricants.
- Issue one notification slip for each sexual partner and emphasize the importance of partner treatment.
- Offer HIV counselling and testing, as per Integrated HIV Guidelines.
- Offer voluntary medical male circumcision.
- Offer pre exposure prophylaxis as per guideline.
- Provide cervical cancer screening during follow-up visit.

text:
### Figure 6: Flow chart for management of lower abdominal pain

Sexually active woman with symptom of lower abdominal pain → Take medical and sexual history and assess risk for exposure to STIs → Genital examination (including bi-manual palpation) and speculum examination (where feasible).
→ Any of the following present? Missed/overdue period; recent delivery/abortion/miscarriage; abdominal guarding and/or rebound tenderness; abnormal vaginal bleeding; abdominal mass.
   - Yes → Refer patient urgently for surgical or gynaecological opinion and assessment. Before referral set up an IV line and apply resuscitative measures if necessary.
   - No → Is there lower abdominal tenderness or cervical motion tenderness?
      - Yes → Manage for PID; test for NG/CT/MG if available*; see patient in 3 days → Patient has improved? (No → Refer patient; Yes → Offer HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services.)
      - No → Any other illness found? (Yes → Manage appropriately; No → Offer HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services.)

* to support partner notification. NG, N. gonorrhoeae; CT, C. trachomatis; MG, M. genitalium.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > Mycoplasma genitalium > Description
text:
## Description

M. genitalium causes symptomatic and asymptomatic urethritis among men and is the etiology of approximately 15%-20% of NGU, 20%-25% of nonchlamydial NGU, and 40% of persistent or recurrent urethritis.
Among women, M. genitalium has been associated with cervicitis, PID, preterm delivery, spontaneous abortion, and infertility, with an approximately twofold increase in the risk for these outcomes among women infected with M. genitalium, infections among women are also frequently asymptomatic.
Rectal infection with M. genitalium has been reported among 1%-26% of MSM and among 3% of women ( 941 ). Rectal infections often are asymptomatic, although higher prevalence of M. genitalium has been reported among men with rectal symptoms. Similarly, although asymptomatic M. genitalium has been detected in the pharynx.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > Mycoplasma genitalium > Diagnostic Considerations
text:
## Diagnostic Considerations

M. genitalium is an extremely slow-growing organism. Culture can take up to 6 months, and technical laboratory capacity is limited to research settings. NAAT for M. genitalium is FDA cleared for use with urine and urethral, penile meatal, endocervical, and vaginal swab samples . M. genitalium should be suspected in cases of persistent or recurrent urethritis or cervicitis and considered for PID.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > Mycoplasma genitalium > Treatment
text:
## Treatment

M. genitalium lacks a cell wall, and thus antibiotics targeting cell-wall biosynthesis (e.g., ß-lactams including penicillins and cephalosporins) are ineffective against this organism. Because of the high rates of macrolide resistance with treatment failures and efficient selection of additional resistance, a 1-g dose of azithromycin should not be used.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.5 Scrotal swelling (SSS) > Clinical features:
text:
## Clinical features:

- The patient usually complains of unilateral pain and swelling of the scrotum with a urethral discharge which develops over 1-2 days
- Scrotal swelling may be seen following trauma or testicular torsion and this required immediate referral for surgical or urological opinion.
- On inspection, the scrotal sac appears distended and on palpation, both testicles and the epididymis are swollen and tender. Differential Dx: Testicular torsion, testicular trauma, inguinal hernia, hydrocele and haematocele

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.6. Inguinal bubo (IBS) > Description
text:
## Description

Inguinal and femoral buboes are localized enlargements of the lymph nodes in the groin area, which are painful and may be fluctuant (soft with a feeling of liquid inside). Inguinal bubo is rarely the sole manifestation of an STI and is usually found together with other genital ulcer disease. Buboes are usually caused by Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) and Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1- L3. Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is an non ulcerative sexually transmitted disease of the genital area caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. It is important to elicit history of recent genital ulcer and examine the external genitalia in all patients presenting with bubos so that effective management can be given.

text:
## Etiology

- Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2 and L3 is a gram negative coccoid or rodshaped bacteria that causes genitourinary tract and eye infection.
- Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) is an ulcerative sexually transmitted disease of the genital area but internal vaginal ulcers in women may be missed and management should follow the flow chart genital ulcer.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.6. Inguinal bubo (IBS) > Clinical features
text:
## Clinical features

- Inguinal buboes can occur as unilateral or bilateral, single or multiple painful swellings. Other STI’s (such as gonorrhoea,
- Syphilis, herpes and HIV) may cause inguinal lymphadenopathy, which may typically be painful (herpes, gonorrhoea) or non-painful (syphilis, HIV).
- If during examination, genital ulcer(s) are seen along with inguinal buboes, the clinical management should follow the genital ulcer syndrome (GUS) protocol.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.6. Inguinal bubo (IBS) > Syndromic treatment of inguinal bubo
text:
## Syndromic treatment of inguinal bubo

- Ceftriaxone, 1 g IM STAT OR Azithromycin, 1g orally STAT and then 1 g orally per week for 2 weeks OR Erythromycin, 500mg orally QID for 14 days OR Ciprofloxacin, 500mg orally BID for 3 days.
LGV:
- Doxycycline, 100mg orally BID for 14 days OR Azithromycin, 1g orally STAT and then 1 g orally per week for 2 weeks OR Erythromycin, 500mg orally QID for 14 days.
- * In patients intolerant to Doxycycline, or pregnant and lactating women: Give 3 doses of Azithromycin, 1 g orally per week or Erythromycin, 500mg orally QID for 14 days
NB: For fluctuant Buboes, refer for aspiration.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.6. Inguinal bubo (IBS) > 5.6.1 Chart 6
text:
### Syndromic treatment chart for inguinal bubo (chart 6)

Client complains of swelling in the groin with or without pain → Take history and examine.
→ Enlarged and/or painful inguinal/femoral bubo(s) present?
   - NO → Any other STI syndrome or illness present? (NO → Reassure, counsel and educate; condom promoted and provided. YES → Treat according to appropriate flow chart.)
   - YES → Azithromycin, 1g orally stat and then 1g orally per week for 2 weeks PLUS Ceftriaxone, 500mg IM stat. For a fluctuant bubo aspiration is vital. Follow up after 7 days.
      → Follow-up at 7 days: improved?
         - YES → Finalise treatment; reinforce health promotion package.
         - NO → Poor compliance with oral therapy? (YES → Repeat treatment; reinforce health promotion package. NO → Refer for further management.)

Health promotion package:
- Educate, ensure compliance, and counsel on treatment.
- Promote abstinence or condom use during treatment.
- Promote correct and consistent condom use also provide condoms and lubricants.
- Issue one notification slip for each sexual partner and emphasize the importance of partner treatment.
- Offer HIV counselling and testing, as per Integrated HIV Guidelines.
- Offer voluntary medical male circumcision.
- Offer pre exposure prophylaxis as per guideline.
- Provide cervical cancer screening during follow-up visit.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.7. Neonatal conjunctivitis > Description
text:
## Description

Neonatal conjunctivitis is the condition where the baby develops purulent conjunctivitis in one or both eyes within four weeks of birth. It is a medical emergency and unless treatment is initiated within 24 hours there could be permanent damage to the eyes resulting in blindness. STI-related infections are passed from the mother to the neonate during vaginal delivery.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.7. Neonatal conjunctivitis > Prevention measures:
html:
Prevention measures:

- Screen all pregnant women for Sexually Transmitted Infections during pregnancy and provide appropriate treatment;

- Routine application of tetracycline eye ointment (1%) to all new-born’s at the time of delivery;

- Provide health promotion package to parents.

- All new-born babies with conjunctivitis should be treated for both N. gonorrhoea and C. trachomatis because of the possibility of mixed infections. Clean the eyes with distilled water or saline.

- Persons caring for infected infants should always wash their hands carefully. Parents (mother and father or partner) should be examined and treated.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.7. Neonatal conjunctivitis > 5.7.1 Chart 7
text:
### Syndromic treatment chart for neonatal conjunctivitis (chart 7)

Neonate with eye(s) discharge → Take history and examine.
→ Swollen eyelid(s) with purulent discharge present?
   - NO → Reassure parent/guardian; advise to return if symptoms persist.
   - YES → Ceftriaxone, 50mg/kg body weight (max. 125mg) IM single dose PLUS Erythromycin syrup, 50mg/kg body weight orally daily in 4 divided doses for 14 days. Provide health promotion package to parents; follow up after 2 days or earlier, if worsening.
      → Follow up at 2 days: improved? (YES → Finalize treatment; reassure parent/guardian. NO → Reassure parent/guardian and refer for further management.)

Health promotion package:
- Educate, ensure compliance, and counsel on treatment.
- Promote abstinence or condom use during treatment.
- Promote correct and consistent condom use also provide condoms and lubricants.
- Issue one notification slip for each sexual partner and emphasize the importance of partner treatment.
- Offer HIV counselling and testing, as per Integrated HIV Guidelines.
- Offer voluntary medical male circumcision.
- Offer pre exposure prophylaxis as per guideline.
